title: Global Risk Governance Monitor: Multilateral Governance of Global Catastrophic and Existential Risks
license: CC BY-NC 4.0. Free to use, share and adapt for non-commercial purposes, provided the origin is cited: Jan Cherlet, globalriskgovernance.org (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/)
citation: Cherlet, J. (2026). RiskGovernance dataset v4.0, Global Risk Governance Monitor, globalriskgovernance.org
companion_dataset: GlobalRisks.json contains the definitions of the risks governed and the assessment of their likelihood and impact.
changes: Version 4.0 (27 November 2026). All text was rewritten in short, full sentences.

Climate change: the climate conference COP31 in Antalya (November 2026) closed without a political decision. The United States has given notice that it will leave the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. New pledges to the climate funds fell. The scores did not change, and the trend remains eroding.
Biosphere collapse: the results of the first global review of the biodiversity targets and of the finance decisions of October 2026 were added. The scores did not change.

Uncontrolled advanced AI: Pax Silica, led by the United States, and the World AI Cooperation Organization, proposed by China, were added. The scores did not change. The trend remains strengthening, with a note on fragmentation.
AI as amplifier: the outcome of the Seventh Review Conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (November 2026) was added. The trend changed from strengthening to stable.
Permanent global power lock-in: a note on the two AI groupings was added.

Structure: maturity levels are now objects with a rule and a meaning. Every risk has a trend label in words. For 'Other WMD', the top-level pillars summarise the two sub-regimes and the top-level scores are their average.

methodology.purpose: For each global catastrophic and existential risk in the companion GlobalRisks dataset, this dataset lists the multilateral institutions and treaties that exist to assess, regulate, finance and enforce the reduction of the risk. It records the coverage, the binding force and the enforcement power of each. From these it derives one indicator per risk: the maturity of multilateral risk governance. The dataset is the governance layer of the Global Risk Governance Monitor (globalriskgovernance.org).

scope.rule: A mechanism is listed if it passes all three tests.
scope.test_1_multilateral: Multilateral. The mechanism is formed by, or open to, states from at least two continents. This includes universal UN bodies, global treaties, clubs that span regions (the OECD, the Australia Group, the Wassenaar Arrangement) and bilateral treaties across continents (arms control between the United States and Russia). It excludes purely national instruments and regional bodies of a single continent. A regional organisation is included where its instruments are open to states from other continents and those states have joined. Examples are the Budapest Convention and the AI convention of the Council of Europe, and the OSCE.
scope.test_2_intergovernmental: Intergovernmental. Governments are the members or the parties. Public-private partnerships (CEPI, Gavi), scientific unions (IAVCEI, IUCN), industry standards bodies and initiatives of non-governmental organisations are mentioned where they fill a gap, but they are not scored. Their presence in place of an intergovernmental body is itself a finding.
scope.test_3_function: Function. The mandate of the mechanism covers the risk explicitly, or a defined part of it. General bodies whose mandate touches the risk only in passing are recorded as generic. They score at most 1 on any pillar.
scope.coverage: Coverage is the number of governments that take part in the mechanism, are party to it or have formally recognised it. There are four bands: Universal (180 states or more), Broad (120 to 179), Partial (60 to 119) and Club (fewer than 60). A note records which critical actors are missing. Critical actors are the states whose behaviour mostly determines the risk.

pillars.basis: The four pillars are the functions that the research on regime effectiveness finds necessary for an international institution to change outcomes. Haas, Keohane and Levy (1993) name three: raising concern through knowledge and monitoring, improving the contractual environment through rules and commitments, and building capacity through finance and assistance. Downs, Rocke and Barsoom (1996) and Mitchell (1994) add the condition of enforcement. The four priorities of the Sendai Framework and the risk-governance cycle of the IRGC follow the same logic.
pillars.assess: Standing intergovernmental bodies that produce authoritative knowledge about the risk and detect or monitor it. Examples are scientific assessment panels, monitoring networks and early-warning systems.
pillars.regulate: Treaties and other instruments that commit states to reduce the risk. Examples are prohibitions, limits, standards, targets and obligations of conduct.
pillars.finance: Dedicated intergovernmental funds or facilities that pay for reducing the risk in advance. Paying for disaster response after the event does not count.
pillars.enforce: Bodies with an independent power to verify compliance and to respond to non-compliance, through inspection, adjudication or sanction.

recorded_fields.type: Treaty, UN organ or agency, assessment panel, fund, club, or soft-law instrument.
recorded_fields.coverage: The number of governments and the coverage band.
recorded_fields.enforcement_powers: Inspection, adjudication, referral or sanction. The effectiveness of their use is rated as proven, partial, weak or untested.

pillar_scoring.scale: Each pillar is scored from 0 to 3 for each risk.
pillar_scoring.0: Assess: nothing dedicated. Regulate: no instrument. Finance: none. Enforce: none.
pillar_scoring.1: Assess: a generic body touches the risk in passing, or there is a one-off study. Regulate: soft law only, or a binding instrument that covers only a small part of the risk. Finance: one-off or general-purpose funding. Enforce: self-reporting or peer review only, without independent verification.
pillar_scoring.2: Assess: a dedicated intergovernmental body that has partial coverage or thin capacity, or is new and untested. Regulate: a binding treaty in force with broad coverage but with weak, voluntary or unverified obligations; or a binding and adequate treaty that is not yet in force or that key actors have not joined. Finance: a dedicated fund that is small compared with the need, or not yet funded. Enforce: independent verification or adjudication without the power to sanction, or with a power that can rarely be used.
pillar_scoring.3: Assess: a standing, dedicated and authoritative body with near-universal membership, and with operational monitoring where the risk allows it. Regulate: binding, substantive and near-universal rules that include the critical actors. Finance: a dedicated fund that is funded and replenished at scale. Enforce: powers of verification and sanction that are used with demonstrable effect.
pillar_scoring.natural_risks: For natural hazards, the Regulate and Enforce pillars measure agreed protocols for prevention and preparedness. Examples are who authorises the deflection of an asteroid, who holds food stocks for a volcanic winter, and which standard applies to the hardening of electricity grids. The scores are not relaxed for natural hazards, because the absence of such protocols is a real gap.

Fully developed.rule: Score 10 to 12, with Regulate at 3, Enforce at 2 or more, and no pillar at 0.
Fully developed.meaning: All four functions are present. The rules bind the actors that matter, and they are verified, financed and enforced.

Developed.rule: Score 7 to 9, with Regulate at 2 or more and no pillar at 0.
Developed.meaning: A binding regime exists with all four functions, but at least one of them is clearly weak.

Developing.rule: Score 4 to 6 with at least one pillar at 2 or more; or any higher score with a pillar at 0; or a regime capped by the critical-actor gate.
Developing.meaning: Real institutions exist, but a function is missing or the regime cannot bind the actors that generate the risk.

Nascent.rule: Score 1 to 3; or score 4 to 6 with no pillar at 2 or more.
Nascent.meaning: There is assessment or dialogue only. No binding instrument is in force on the risk itself.

Non-existent.meaning: There is no dedicated mechanism of any kind.

maturity_indicator.critical_actor_gate: Maturity is capped at Developing, whatever the score, in two cases. The first is where the states whose behaviour mostly determines the risk are not bound by the substantive obligations of the regime. The second is where those states are structurally immune from its enforcement, for example through the veto of a permanent member of the Security Council.

trend.basis: The trend is judged on events from 2024 to 2026.

maturity_indicator.interpretation: The maturity level describes the architecture of the regime. Its effectiveness is shown by the Enforce score and by the note 'in practice' for each risk. Both are given, so that a Developed regime that performs poorly is not mistaken for one that performs well.

benchmark.name: Stratospheric ozone depletion (a benchmark, not a current risk)

assess.mechanisms: Three assessment panels have reported every four years since 1989: the Scientific Assessment Panel, the Environmental Effects Assessment Panel and the Technology and Economic Assessment Panel. The WMO and UNEP monitor the ozone layer.

regulate.mechanisms: The Vienna Convention (1985), the Montreal Protocol (1987) and the Kigali Amendment (2016).
regulate.coverage: 198 parties. These are the only treaties in UN history that every state has ratified. The Kigali Amendment has more than 160 parties.
regulate.status: Binding and verified. The controls can be adjusted and have been tightened nine times.

finance.mechanisms: The Multilateral Fund, created in 1991.
finance.status: About US$5 billion has been paid out. The replenishment for 2024 to 2026 is US$965 million.

enforce.mechanisms: The Ozone Secretariat, an Implementation Committee with a non-compliance procedure, and trade restrictions with non-parties under Article 4 of the Protocol.
enforce.status: Compliance is verified through mandatory reporting, and trade sanctions are available. The powers have been used. In 2018 and 2019, atmospheric monitoring detected illegal production of CFC-11, and the case was resolved.

benchmark.note: Ozone depletion was a real global catastrophic risk in the 1980s and was resolved by governance. It is the yardstick for the level Fully developed. Five ingredients come together: binding rules, independent verification, universal membership, a financed transition and rules that can be adjusted.

methodology.verification: Membership, ratification and status figures were verified against primary sources up to 16 September 2026. The entries on climate change, biosphere collapse, uncontrolled advanced AI and AI as amplifier were updated to 27 November 2026 from UN documents and specialist reporting. Approximate counts are marked 'about'. To be verified again at the next update: the outcome of the Review Conference of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (November to December 2026); the number of parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change after the United States leaves on 27 February 2027; the membership and legal status of the World AI Cooperation Organization and of Pax Silica; the work of the expert group on autonomous weapons in 2027 and 2028; the ratifications of the UN Convention against Cybercrime and of the High Seas Treaty; and the annex to the WHO Pandemic Agreement (target May 2027).

risks.name: Asteroid / comet impact

assess.mechanisms: The International Asteroid Warning Network (IAWN) was endorsed by the UN General Assembly in 2013 (resolution 68/75) and is chaired by NASA. The Space Mission Planning Advisory Group (SMPAG) is chaired by the European Space Agency. The UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS) has 104 member states.
assess.coverage: IAWN: about 60 institutions in about 25 countries. SMPAG: about 20 space agencies. COPUOS: partial to broad.
assess.status: Detection works: about 95% of objects of 1 km or more are catalogued. The procedures were tested in 2025 for asteroid 2024 YR4. Capacity is concentrated in the United States, Europe and Japan.

regulate.mechanisms: The Outer Space Treaty (1967, 115 parties) governs activities in space but says nothing about planetary defence. No protocol states who may authorise or command the deflection of an object.
regulate.binding_or_powers: Binding, but not on this risk
regulate.status: Deflection is technically proven by NASA's DART mission (2022), and the European Hera mission arrives at the same asteroid in 2026. The decision to deflect has no legal home.

finance.mechanisms: None. Missions are paid for nationally, by NASA, the European Space Agency and Japan's space agency.

enforce.mechanisms: None.

risks.in_practice: This is the best-understood risk in the Monitor, but it is governed only on the knowledge side. In the UN Global Risk Report 2026, respondents expect a space-based event only after eight years and name gaps in data as the barrier.
risks.gap: There is no agreed protocol, mandate or fund for the decision to respond. Long-period comets are not surveyed well enough.

risks.name: Supervolcanic eruption

assess.mechanisms: The UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction covers hazards in general in its Global Assessment Report. The Volcanic Ash Advisory Centres of the International Civil Aviation Organization cover volcanic ash for aviation only. Scientific unions such as IAVCEI, the World Organization of Volcano Observatories and the Global Volcano Model, and the national Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program, are not intergovernmental and are not scored.
assess.status: No intergovernmental body monitors supervolcanic systems as a global catastrophic hazard.

regulate.mechanisms: The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030 was adopted by 187 states and endorsed by the UN General Assembly (resolution 69/283). It covers disaster risk in general.
regulate.status: Nothing addresses the defining threat: the failure of harvests worldwide for several years.

finance.mechanisms: None. The trust fund of the UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction is general and small.

enforce.mechanisms: None.

risks.in_practice: The hazard cannot be prevented, and it is almost ungoverned.
risks.gap: There is no mandate to monitor, no contingency plan for the food system (strategic reserves, planning for resilient foods) and no fund.
risks.maturity_note: For the global-scale scenario, governance is in effect non-existent.

risks.name: Severe space weather

assess.mechanisms: The World Meteorological Organization (193 members) coordinates space-weather services. Since 2019 the International Civil Aviation Organization has run global space-weather advisory centres. They are operated by the United States, the European PECASUS consortium, the ACFJ consortium (Australia, Canada, France and Japan) and a consortium of China and Russia. The International Space Environment Service links regional warning centres in about 20 countries on five continents. COPUOS has an Expert Group on Space Weather.
assess.coverage: Universal (WMO, ICAO); club (International Space Environment Service)
assess.status: Short-term forecasting is good. The monitoring spacecraft are national assets.

regulate.mechanisms: The standards on space-weather advisories in Annex 3 of the Chicago Convention are binding on 193 states, but they apply to aviation only. No standard exists for electricity grids, satellites or telecommunications. The standards of the International Electrotechnical Commission are voluntary.
regulate.binding_or_powers: Binding on a small part of the risk
regulate.status: The hardening of grids is a national matter and is uneven.

finance.mechanisms: None.

enforce.mechanisms: None for this risk. The safety audits of the International Civil Aviation Organization cover aviation only and carry no sanctions.

risks.in_practice: Forecasting is governed. The systems at risk are not.
risks.gap: No binding resilience standard protects grids and critical infrastructure against a storm of Carrington size. The UN Global Risk Report 2026 lists the space-based event among the risks with a data gap.

risks.name: Natural pandemic

assess.mechanisms: The World Health Organization has 193 members since the withdrawal of the United States took effect in January 2026, and Argentina has announced that it will withdraw. Its detection system includes the WHO Hub for Pandemic and Epidemic Intelligence in Berlin (2021), the Global Outbreak Alert and Response Network, the Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System (since 1952) and the notification of events under the International Health Regulations. The WHO works with the FAO, the World Organisation for Animal Health and UNEP on One Health.
assess.status: This is the strongest detection architecture of any risk in the Monitor.

regulate.mechanisms: The International Health Regulations (2005) are binding on 196 states parties. Amendments adopted in 2024 added a new alert level, the 'pandemic emergency', and provisions on equity. They entered into force on 19 September 2025 for the states that did not reject them. The United States rejected them. The WHO Pandemic Agreement was adopted on 20 May 2025 (resolution WHA78.1, by 124 votes to 0 with 11 abstentions). It will be binding once it is in force. It opens for signature only after an annex on Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing is adopted. The deadline of May 2026 was missed, and the new target is May 2027.
regulate.binding_or_powers: Binding, but the obligations are mostly procedural (notification, core capacities). The Pandemic Agreement is adopted but not in force.
regulate.status: The exit of the United States has dented universality.

finance.mechanisms: The Pandemic Fund, hosted by the World Bank since 2022, has received more than US$2 billion, against an estimated need of US$10 billion a year. The WHO also has a Contingency Fund for Emergencies. Two partnerships are not scored because they are not intergovernmental: CEPI (US$3.5 billion) and Gavi, whose replenishment for 2026 to 2030 raised about US$9 billion, below its target.

enforce.mechanisms: The Emergency Committee under the International Health Regulations advises on declaring a public health emergency of international concern. The 2024 amendments created an Implementation Committee that reviews compliance in a facilitative way. There is no inspection and no sanction.
enforce.status: COVID-19 showed that delays in notification have no consequences.

risks.in_practice: The system detects well and complies weakly. In the UN Global Risk Report 2026, pandemics and biological risks are outside the top ten of every region. The report itself warns against this shift in attention.
risks.gap: There is no leverage to secure compliance. The bargain on pathogen access and equity is unfinished. Financing is a fraction of the need. A major power is outside the WHO.
risks.maturity_note: The trend would turn upward if the Pandemic Agreement enters into force. The exit of the United States pulls it down. The net result is stable.

risks.name: Climate change

assess.mechanisms: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has 195 members and is working on its seventh assessment cycle. The World Meteorological Organization runs the Global Atmosphere Watch and publishes the State of the Climate reports. The Global Climate Observing System and the Emissions Gap Report of UNEP complete the picture.
assess.status: Exemplary. It is the model that every other risk borrows.

regulate.mechanisms: The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (1992) has 198 parties. The Paris Agreement (2015) has 194 parties since the withdrawal of the United States took effect on 27 January 2026. In February 2026 the United States also gave notice that it will leave the Framework Convention itself on 27 February 2027. The climate conference COP31 in Antalya (9 to 22 November 2026) closed without its main political decision. At least 32 countries rejected the draft 'Antalya Pact' because it did not mention fossil fuels. The decision on the mitigation work programme was also blocked. Technical decisions on adaptation, the Adaptation Fund and just transition were adopted.
regulate.binding_or_powers: Binding on procedure (submitting national plans and reporting on them). The content of the national plans and the temperature goal of 1.5 to 2 °C are not binding.
regulate.status: The national plans submitted in 2025 fall short of a 1.5 °C pathway. In 2026 the parties could not agree on a political response.

finance.mechanisms: The Green Climate Fund received pledges of US$13.6 billion for its second replenishment, and about US$30 billion has been pledged to it since 2010. Other funds are the climate window of the Global Environment Facility, the Adaptation Fund and the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (2023). About US$0.8 billion has been pledged to the loss and damage fund, of which about US$0.5 billion had been paid in by July 2026, against funding requests of US$2.8 billion. In 2024 the conference COP29 set a new goal of US$300 billion a year by 2035. In 2026, new pledges to the UN climate funds fell to their lowest level in years.
finance.status: This is the largest dedicated finance architecture of any risk. It is still far below the need, and new pledges are falling.

enforce.mechanisms: The Enhanced Transparency Framework of the Paris Agreement requires reports every two years, which technical experts review. The Implementation and Compliance Committee is facilitative and cannot punish. Courts are opening a new route. In an advisory opinion of 23 July 2025, the International Court of Justice found that states have binding obligations to prevent significant harm to the climate. In 2024 the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea found that greenhouse gases are a form of marine pollution.

risks.in_practice: The architecture is comprehensive, but the outcomes are weak. Emissions remain above the agreed pathway. In November 2026 the annual conference closed without a political agreement, although several technical decisions were adopted. In the UN Global Risk Report 2026, climate change is still the most important risk and among the three best prepared for, which refers to identifying the risk and not to reducing it.
risks.gap: Nobody enforces national targets. Finance is far below the need. The second-largest emitter is outside the regime. In 2026 the parties could not agree to name fossil fuels. This is a gap in effectiveness, not in architecture.
risks.maturity_note: The United States has left the Paris Agreement and is leaving the Framework Convention. The 2026 conference ended without a political outcome.

risks.name: Biosphere collapse

assess.mechanisms: The Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) has about 150 members. The FAO reports on forests, fisheries, soil and water. UNEP publishes the Global Environment Outlook, and the UN Convention to Combat Desertification publishes the Global Land Outlook. The Red List of the IUCN is not scored, because the IUCN is not purely intergovernmental. In October 2026 the first global review under the Convention on Biological Diversity found the world behind on 22 of the 23 targets for 2030.
assess.status: Strong on biodiversity. Thin on fresh water and soil as global risks.

regulate.mechanisms: The Convention on Biological Diversity (1993) has 196 parties; the United States is not one of them. Its Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022) sets 23 voluntary targets, including the protection of 30% of land and sea by 2030. Other treaties are CITES on trade in endangered species (185 parties, binding trade rules), the Ramsar Convention on wetlands (172), the Convention on Migratory Species (133) and the Convention to Combat Desertification (197). The High Seas Treaty entered into force on 17 January 2026 and has more than 70 parties. Pollution is covered by the Basel (191), Stockholm (186), Rotterdam (167) and Minamata (about 150) conventions. The UN Watercourses Convention has only 38 parties. Negotiations on a global plastics treaty failed to reach agreement in Geneva in August 2025 and continue.
regulate.coverage: Universal (Convention on Biological Diversity, without the United States)
regulate.binding_or_powers: Binding frameworks with voluntary targets (biodiversity). Binding rules by sector (trade in species, chemicals).
regulate.status: The Aichi targets for 2010 to 2020 were almost all missed. The review of October 2026 warns that the 2030 targets will not be met unless action speeds up.

finance.mechanisms: The Global Environment Facility funds biodiversity; its eighth funding round totals US$5.3 billion for all areas. The Global Biodiversity Framework Fund (2023) holds about US$0.4 billion. China's Kunming Biodiversity Fund holds US$230 million. The Cali Fund (2024) should collect payments from companies that use genetic sequence data; it held less than US$9,000 in October 2026. The target of US$20 billion a year in international flows by 2025 was missed. The target for 2030 is US$200 billion a year from all sources. In October 2026 the parties agreed to set up a financial mechanism under the Convention for the period after 2030, but left its form to their next conference in 2028.
finance.status: Dedicated, but about ten times too small.

enforce.mechanisms: CITES has a compliance procedure with trade suspensions. It is used and it works, but it covers a narrow field. The Convention on Biological Diversity relies on reporting and review only. The chemicals conventions have compliance committees without sanctions.

risks.in_practice: The architecture exists on paper, the targets are missed and the finance lags behind. In the UN Global Risk Report 2026, biodiversity and pollution fell most in perceived importance and imminence.
risks.gap: The targets are voluntary. Finance is far short. The United States is absent. No global regime covers fresh water or soil. The plastics treaty is unresolved.
risks.maturity_note: The score is at the bottom of the band for Developed.

risks.name: Nuclear war

assess.mechanisms: The International Atomic Energy Agency (180 members) applies safeguards under 182 comprehensive safeguards agreements; the Additional Protocol is in force for about 142 states. The International Monitoring System of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization has 337 facilities and operates although the treaty is not in force. In December 2024 the UN General Assembly created an independent Scientific Panel on the Effects of Nuclear War (resolution 79/238). Its 21 experts were appointed in July 2025 and will report in 2027. It is the first such study since 1988. The UN Institute for Disarmament Research and the UN Scientific Committee on the Effects of Atomic Radiation also contribute.
assess.status: The monitoring of proliferation and testing is world-class. The monitoring of the risk of war is only now being built.

regulate.mechanisms: The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (1970) has 191 parties. India, Israel and Pakistan never joined, and North Korea withdrew in 2003. The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (1996) has 187 signatures and about 178 ratifications but is not in force: nine states whose ratification is required are missing, and Russia revoked its ratification in November 2023. The Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (2021) has 75 states parties (July 2026) and 25 further signatories. No nuclear-armed state has joined it. Its first Review Conference takes place in November and December 2026. Five treaties create nuclear-weapon-free zones that cover about 116 states. Security Council resolution 1540 binds all 193 UN members to keep such weapons from non-state actors. The Nuclear Suppliers Group (48 members) coordinates export controls. Between the United States and Russia, the New START treaty expired on 5 February 2026 without a successor and without negotiations. For the first time since 1972, no treaty limits the two largest arsenals. The INF Treaty ended in 2019 and the Open Skies Treaty in 2020 and 2021.
regulate.binding_or_powers: Binding and verified on non-proliferation. The disarmament obligation of Article VI is not enforced. No binding limit applies to any arsenal. The test ban rests on custom only.
regulate.status: All nine states with nuclear weapons are outside any numerical limit. China is in no arms-control framework.

finance.mechanisms: The regular budget and the Technical Cooperation Fund of the International Atomic Energy Agency pay for verification and safety, not for reducing the risk of war. The test-ban organisation has its own budget. No fund exists for arms control or risk reduction.
finance.status: The money finances verification, not risk reduction.

enforce.mechanisms: The Board of the International Atomic Energy Agency can refer a state to the UN Security Council, as it did with Iran in 2006 and with North Korea. The Council has imposed sanctions on North Korea since 2006 (resolution 1718). UN sanctions on Iran were re-imposed through the 'snapback' mechanism on 28 September 2025. The Agency carries out inspections.
enforce.status: Partly effective. North Korea acquired weapons while under sanctions. Iran's programme was met with military strikes in June 2025, not with compliance.

risks.in_practice: The regime governs who may acquire nuclear weapons far better than whether the states that have them use them. The layer that limited arsenals has lapsed. In the UN Global Risk Report 2026, weapons of mass destruction re-entered the top ten risks in three regions, and large-scale war is the major risk for which the world is least prepared.
risks.gap: There are no limits on arsenals. There are no rules on AI in nuclear command and control. The test-ban treaty is not in force. The states with nuclear weapons are outside the prohibition treaty.

risks.name: Engineered pandemic

assess.mechanisms: The Implementation Support Unit of the Biological Weapons Convention has four staff. A scientific and technological advisory mechanism was recommended by the working group of 2023 to 2026 but does not exist yet. The working group was extended into 2026, and the decision falls to the Tenth Review Conference in 2027. The UN Secretary-General's Mechanism can investigate alleged use, with experts drawn from a roster when needed. Outbreaks are detected through the WHO systems described under natural pandemic, but these cannot attribute an outbreak to an actor. The WHO Global Guidance Framework for the Responsible Use of the Life Sciences (2022) is soft law.
assess.status: No standing body assesses dual-use biology or biology enabled by AI.

regulate.mechanisms: The Biological Weapons Convention (1975) has 189 states parties and contains a binding prohibition. It has no verification body: negotiations on a verification protocol collapsed in 2001. The Geneva Protocol of 1925 has 146 parties. Security Council resolution 1540 binds all 193 UN members. The Australia Group (43 members) is a voluntary club for export controls. The Cartagena Protocol (173 parties) covers the biosafety of living modified organisms, not weapons.
regulate.binding_or_powers: Binding but not verified. Nothing covers dual-use research, laboratory biosafety or the design of pathogens with AI.
regulate.status: The critical actors are inside the Convention, but their compliance cannot be verified.

finance.mechanisms: No dedicated fund exists. A fund for international cooperation and assistance under the Convention has been proposed but not created. The Pandemic Fund and the trust fund for resolution 1540 touch the risk only in passing.

enforce.mechanisms: Under Article VI of the Convention a state can complain to the Security Council; this has never been done. Confidence-building measures are voluntary, and about half of the parties submit them. The Secretary-General's Mechanism has investigated chemical allegations but never a biological one.

risks.in_practice: The prohibition is fifty years old and has no way to detect cheating. It now faces a technology that removes the barrier of expertise. In the UN Global Risk Report 2026, biological risks fell in perceived importance in every region.
risks.gap: Four things are missing: verification, the governance of dual-use research and of biology enabled by AI, a dedicated assessment body, and any finance.

risks.name: Other WMD (chemical, radiological)

assess.mechanisms: For chemical weapons, the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons has a standing Technical Secretariat and a Scientific Advisory Board. For radioactive material, the International Atomic Energy Agency keeps an Incident and Trafficking Database. The details are given for each sub-regime.
assess.status: Strong for chemical weapons, thinner for radioactive material.

regulate.mechanisms: The Chemical Weapons Convention (193 parties) bans chemical weapons and is verified. Radioactive material is covered by conventions on physical protection and on nuclear terrorism, and by a voluntary code of conduct on radioactive sources.
regulate.status: All declared chemical stockpiles were destroyed by July 2023. The security of radioactive sources is uneven.

finance.mechanisms: The chemical regime is paid for from the budget of its organisation and from trust funds. The radiological regime relies on the voluntary Nuclear Security Fund.
finance.status: Adequate for chemical weapons, small for radioactive material.

enforce.mechanisms: The chemical regime has inspections, the attribution of use and the suspension of rights, and it has used them. The radiological regime has advisory missions on invitation only.
enforce.status: Proven for chemical weapons, absent for radioactive material.

risks.scores_note: Each pillar score is the average of the chemical and radiological sub-regimes.
risks.in_practice: The chemical-weapons regime is the only current regime in the Monitor that reaches the level Fully developed. The regime for radioactive material is weaker and has no right of inspection.
risks.gap: Two things are missing: the security of radioactive sources with an independent right of inspection, and enforcement against a state that defies the chemical regime under the protection of a great power.
risks.maturity_note: The score of 9 is the average of the chemical sub-regime (11, Fully developed) and the radiological sub-regime (7, Developed).

assess.mechanisms: The Technical Secretariat and the Scientific Advisory Board of the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), together with the system of declarations by states.

regulate.mechanisms: The Chemical Weapons Convention (1997) has 193 states parties. Egypt, North Korea and South Sudan are outside, and Israel has signed but not ratified.
regulate.status: All declared stockpiles (72,000 tonnes) have been destroyed. Destruction was completed in July 2023.

finance.mechanisms: The regular budget of the OPCW, assistance under Article X of the Convention, and voluntary trust funds, such as the one for the destruction of Syria's chemical weapons in 2013 and 2014.
finance.status: There is no standing fund for reduction, but destruction was financed when it was needed.

enforce.mechanisms: The OPCW carries out routine inspections and, on request, challenge inspections. Its Investigation and Identification Team attributes the use of chemical weapons, as it did in Syria. In 2021 the Conference of the States Parties suspended Syria's rights. Cases can be referred to the UN Security Council or General Assembly, but Russia has vetoed action in the Council.
enforce.status: Proven. The OPCW received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2013. The limits show when a state defies the regime under the protection of a great power.

assess.mechanisms: The Incident and Trafficking Database of the International Atomic Energy Agency (about 145 states) and the Agency's Nuclear Security Series of guidance.

regulate.mechanisms: The Convention on the Physical Protection of Nuclear Material (1987, 164 parties) and its 2005 Amendment (in force since 2016, about 135 parties). The International Convention for the Suppression of Acts of Nuclear Terrorism (2005, about 125 parties). The Code of Conduct on the Safety and Security of Radioactive Sources of the International Atomic Energy Agency (2004), to which about 145 states have made a political commitment.
regulate.binding_or_powers: Binding on physical protection; soft law on radioactive sources
regulate.status: The security of radioactive sources is uneven.

finance.mechanisms: The Nuclear Security Fund of the International Atomic Energy Agency, which is voluntary and receives about €40 million a year.

enforce.mechanisms: The advisory missions of the International Atomic Energy Agency on physical protection take place only on invitation. There is no right of inspection and no sanction.

risks.name: Uncontrolled advanced AI

assess.mechanisms: The UN General Assembly created the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI in August 2025 (resolution 79/325). Its 40 experts presented a first report at the Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva on 6 and 7 July 2026. The report finds that there is 'no technical guarantee' that frontier systems follow instructions. The next Dialogue takes place in New York on 3 and 4 May 2027. The International AI Safety Report, chaired by Yoshua Bengio, is written by experts nominated by about 33 governments, the European Union, the UN and the OECD. The International Network of AI Safety and Security Institutes has 10 members: the United States, the United Kingdom, Japan, South Korea, Singapore, Canada, Australia, France, Kenya and the European Union. China is not a member. The OECD runs an AI Policy Observatory.
assess.status: New, thin and promising. It is an 'IPCC for AI' in its first year.

regulate.mechanisms: No binding instrument covers the safety of frontier models or the loss of control. The Framework Convention on AI of the Council of Europe (2024) is the first binding AI treaty. It has about 19 signatories, including the United States, the United Kingdom, the European Union, Canada, Japan, Israel and Switzerland. It has one ratification (the European Union, 15 May 2026) and needs five, including three member states of the Council of Europe, to enter into force. It protects rights and excludes national security. Soft law includes the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI (2021, 193 states), the OECD AI Principles (47 adherents), two resolutions of the UN General Assembly (78/265 and 78/311, 2024), the Global Digital Compact (2024) and the code of conduct of the G7 Hiroshima Process. Sixteen companies made private Frontier AI Safety Commitments in Seoul in 2024. Two rival groupings have formed around the leading AI powers. Pax Silica, led by the United States, was launched on 12 December 2025 with a non-binding declaration, which about 25 governments had signed by November 2026. It aims to secure the supply chains for chips, AI and critical minerals among partners. On 15 November 2026, ten of them signed the San Francisco Declaration, which sets up working groups and contains no safety rules. The World AI Cooperation Organization (WAICO), proposed by China, was founded in Shanghai on 16 July 2026 by 29 states, including Russia, Brazil, Indonesia and South Africa. No Western state joined. It promotes cooperation and capacity-building and sets no safety rules.
regulate.type: Treaty (not in force), soft law, clubs
regulate.coverage: Club (binding treaty, Pax Silica, WAICO); universal (soft law)
regulate.binding_or_powers: Soft law. The one binding treaty is not in force and does not cover this risk.
regulate.status: The United States and China hold about 90% of frontier computing power. They are bound by no safety rule, and each now leads its own grouping.

finance.mechanisms: None. The Global Fund for AI proposed in the Global Digital Compact is for capacity-building, not for safety.

enforce.mechanisms: None.

risks.in_practice: Scientific assessment arrived in 2025 and 2026. Governance is now emerging on three separate tracks: a universal UN track that assesses and discusses, a grouping led by the United States and an organisation led by China. None of them sets safety rules for frontier AI. In the UN Global Risk Report 2026, this risk shows the sharpest rise in perceived importance, preparedness ranks 24th of 28, and a gap in data is the stated barrier.
risks.gap: Compared with the size of the risk, this is the largest gap in the Monitor. There are no safety rules, no oversight of frontier development or of computing power, no fund and no enforcement. The split into rival groupings makes universal rules harder to reach.
risks.maturity_note: More institutions exist than a year ago, but they are dividing along geopolitical lines.

risks.name: Failed geoengineering

assess.mechanisms: The IPCC assessed solar radiation modification in its sixth assessment report. UNEP reviewed it in the report One Atmosphere (2023). The Scientific Assessment Panel of the Montreal Protocol was mandated in 2023 (decisions XXXV/3 and XXXV/4) to assess the effects of stratospheric aerosols on the ozone layer. The World Meteorological Organization also contributes.
assess.status: The risk is assessed inside other regimes. There is no dedicated body.

regulate.mechanisms: The ENMOD Convention (1978, 78 parties) bans only the hostile use of environmental modification. A decision of the Convention on Biological Diversity (X/33, 2010) amounts to a moratorium in practice, but it is not binding and the United States is not a party. Under the London Convention and Protocol, a 2008 resolution on ocean fertilisation is not binding, and a 2013 amendment on marine geoengineering is not in force: it has 6 of the roughly 36 acceptances needed. Draft resolutions on solar radiation modification were withdrawn at the UN Environment Assembly in 2019 and 2024. The African Ministerial Conference on the Environment called for a global non-use agreement in 2023 and 2025. Nothing governs the injection of aerosols into the stratosphere, the thresholds for research or the danger of a termination shock.
regulate.binding_or_powers: Binding on a small part of the risk; otherwise none

finance.mechanisms: None.

enforce.mechanisms: None.

risks.in_practice: The technology is advancing faster than any rule for it. In the UN Global Risk Report 2026, preparedness ranks 27th of 28, the second lowest, and respondents expect the risk only after eight years.
risks.gap: There is no rule on deployment or research, no non-use agreement, no fund and no enforcement.

risks.name: Unknown unknowns

assess.mechanisms: The UN Global Risk Report appears every two years (2024, 2026) under the Executive Office of the Secretary-General. The UN Futures Lab and the UN University do foresight work. In the Pact for the Future (2024) and its Declaration on Future Generations, states committed to strategic foresight, and a Special Envoy for Future Generations has been proposed.
assess.status: Foresight exists as a function, not as an institution.

regulate.mechanisms: None.

finance.mechanisms: None.

enforce.mechanisms: None.

risks.in_practice: Foresight is carried out in reports and offices. No institution is responsible for acting on what they find.
risks.gap: No standing and funded mechanism exists to identify hazards early and to govern them before they mature.

risks.name: Permanent global power lock-in

assess.mechanisms: The UN Scientific Panel on AI documents the concentration of computing power. UNCTAD reports on technology and competition. The Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and the Human Rights Council monitor civic space and rights. The OECD keeps statistics on competition and tax.
assess.status: No body assesses the concentration of power as a catastrophic risk.

regulate.mechanisms: There is no global competition law. The UN Set of Principles on Restrictive Business Practices (1980) is not binding. The International Competition Network links more than 140 agencies but is soft. The two-pillar tax deal of the OECD and G20 Inclusive Framework covers 147 jurisdictions: its first pillar is dead, and its second pillar was weakened in January 2026 by a 'side-by-side' arrangement that exempts groups with a parent company in the United States. A UN Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation is under negotiation until 2027; its terms of reference were adopted by 110 votes to 8 with 43 abstentions. For the final form of this risk, the relevant treaties are the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (174 parties), which binds states to protect political freedoms, and the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court. The Statute has 124 parties since Hungary's withdrawal took effect in June 2026; the United States, China, Russia and India are outside. The UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights are soft law, and a binding treaty on business and human rights has been under negotiation since 2014. The two groupings that formed around AI in 2025 and 2026, Pax Silica and the World AI Cooperation Organization, organise technology blocs. Neither limits concentration.
regulate.binding_or_powers: Soft on concentration. Binding only on rights, which address the risk indirectly.
regulate.status: The critical actors are the two states and the few companies that control frontier computing power. Nothing binds them on concentration.

finance.mechanisms: The UN Democracy Fund spends about US$5 million a year and is general in purpose.

enforce.mechanisms: The International Criminal Court prosecutes individuals, but its warrants are not enforced against major powers. The International Court of Justice hears disputes between states. The views of the Human Rights Committee and the Universal Periodic Review are peer review without sanction.

risks.in_practice: This is one of the least governed risks. In the UN Global Risk Report 2026, its importance rose sharply and preparedness ranks 22nd of 28.
risks.gap: Nothing addresses the concentration of transformative technology, monopoly power or the pathway to lock-in. The small part covered by tax rules is shrinking.
risks.maturity_note: The tax pillar was weakened in 2026.

risks.name: Civilisational systems collapse

assess.mechanisms: Finance is monitored by the Financial Stability Board (24 jurisdictions and international organisations), the International Monetary Fund (191 members, with country surveillance, financial-sector assessments and the Global Financial Stability Report) and the Bank for International Settlements. Cyber risks are discussed in the UN Global Mechanism on security in the use of information and communication technologies (2025), the permanent successor to an open-ended working group, and at the International Telecommunication Union. Food is monitored by the FAO, the Agricultural Market Information System of the G20 and the Global Network Against Food Crises. Energy is monitored by the International Energy Agency (31 members). Disaster risk is covered by the Global Assessment Report of the UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction.
assess.coverage: Universal (IMF); club (Financial Stability Board, International Energy Agency)
assess.status: Strong sector by sector. Nobody assesses how a failure cascades across sectors.

regulate.mechanisms: The Articles of Agreement of the International Monetary Fund bind 191 members. The Basel III banking standards are soft law for 28 jurisdictions. The rules of the World Trade Organization bind 166 members. Sectoral safety regimes are binding and universal: the International Maritime Organization, the International Civil Aviation Organization and the Radio Regulations of the International Telecommunication Union. The UN Convention against Cybercrime was adopted in December 2024 and has 77 signatories (76 states and the European Union) but only 3 of the 40 ratifications it needs to enter into force. The Budapest Convention on Cybercrime has about 81 parties, including the United States, Japan, Canada, Australia and Argentina. The eleven UN norms of responsible state behaviour in cyberspace and the Sendai Framework are not binding. No binding standard covers the interdependence or resilience of critical infrastructure.
regulate.binding_or_powers: Binding in finance, trade and transport. Soft or not in force elsewhere.

finance.mechanisms: The International Monetary Fund can lend about US$1 trillion. Regional financing arrangements and central-bank swap lines complete the Global Financial Safety Net. The World Bank has crisis facilities, and the UN has the Central Emergency Response Fund. All of these react to a crisis. Nothing pays in advance for resilience across sectors.
finance.status: This is liquidity for crises, not risk reduction.

enforce.mechanisms: The dispute settlement of the World Trade Organization is impaired: its Appellate Body has not functioned since 2019, and an interim appeal arrangement covers about 57 members. The International Monetary Fund attaches conditions to its loans. The Financial Stability Board and the Basel Committee use peer reviews. The International Maritime Organization and the International Civil Aviation Organization carry out mandatory audits without sanctions.

risks.in_practice: Financial shocks from which the world can recover are well governed. The sectoral safety regimes are among the best-governed systems in the world: the safety conventions of shipping and aviation, the Radio Regulations and the obligation of members of the International Energy Agency to hold oil stocks for 90 days are binding, near-universal and audited. But nobody governs the interdependence between these systems, which is what makes this risk possible. The irreversible cascade across sectors has no owner. In the UN Global Risk Report 2026, worry about a financial crisis rose, a supply-chain collapse is now expected in the near term, and preparedness for a cybersecurity breakdown ranks 26th of 28.
risks.gap: No regime covers a polycrisis or the interdependence of infrastructure as a whole. The cybercrime convention is not in force.
risks.maturity_note: The financial channel alone would reach the level Developed.

risks.name: Great-power rivalry

assess.mechanisms: The UN Secretariat provides early warning through its Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs. The Security Council deliberates. The Conflict Prevention Centre of the OSCE serves 57 states on three continents. The UN Register of Conventional Arms is voluntary and receives about 60 reports a year. The UN Institute for Disarmament Research provides analysis.
assess.status: Early warning exists. Transparency on arms is declining.

regulate.mechanisms: The UN Charter (193 members) prohibits the use of force in Article 2(4). The rule is binding and universal. The Geneva Conventions (196 parties) and their Protocols regulate the conduct of war. The Arms Trade Treaty has 116 parties; the United States withdrew its signature, and Russia and China are outside. The Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons has 128 parties. The OSCE has the Vienna Document on military transparency. No conventional or strategic arms control between the great powers remains in force: the Treaty on Conventional Armed Forces in Europe is suspended, the Open Skies Treaty has collapsed and New START has expired.
regulate.coverage: Universal (Charter, humanitarian law); partial (Arms Trade Treaty)
regulate.binding_or_powers: Binding on the use of force. Nothing covers rivalry, arms races or the management of escalation.
regulate.status: The critical actors are the five permanent members of the Security Council.

finance.mechanisms: The UN Peacebuilding Fund spends about US$200 million a year. UN peacekeeping is paid for by assessed contributions of about US$5.6 billion, which were cut in 2026. Both pay for stabilisation after conflict, not for preventing war between great powers.
finance.status: The money is dedicated to conflict, not to rivalry.

enforce.mechanisms: Under Chapter VII of the Charter, the Security Council can impose binding sanctions and authorise force. The veto makes this impossible against a permanent member or a state that it protects. The International Court of Justice has compulsory jurisdiction over 74 states, and its judgments are enforced through the Council. The International Criminal Court has 124 parties; its jurisdiction over aggression is narrow, and the major powers are outside.
enforce.binding_or_powers: The power exists but cannot be used where it matters most.
enforce.status: Weak and declining, as Ukraine and Gaza show.

risks.in_practice: On paper this is the most complete architecture, and it was designed for exactly this risk. By design it cannot act when a great power is the aggressor. In the UN Global Risk Report 2026, geopolitical tensions are among the three risks that are best identified, preparedness for large-scale war fell fastest, and 'weak governance or coordination mechanisms' is the top barrier for every risk.
risks.gap: The veto blocks enforcement. There is no arms control between great powers and no mechanism to manage escalation. The four drivers of rivalry named in the UN Global Risk Report 2026 (resource shortages, economic fragmentation, misinformation and institutional decay) each fall under other, weaker regimes.

risks.name: Social fragmentation, disinformation, governance failure

assess.mechanisms: UNESCO (194 members) monitors media and information. The UN Global Principles for Information Integrity (June 2024) set out expectations. The Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights monitors rights. The UN Global Risk Report is itself an assessment. Indices such as V-Dem and Freedom House, and the Inter-Parliamentary Union, are not bodies of governments and are not scored.
assess.status: No intergovernmental body assesses the integrity of the information environment or the decay of institutions as risks.

regulate.mechanisms: The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (174 parties) is binding. Its Article 19 protects expression and its Article 20 prohibits incitement. The Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination has 182 parties. The Global Digital Compact (2024) and the UNESCO Guidelines for the Governance of Digital Platforms (2023) are soft law. The Budapest Convention and the UN Convention against Cybercrime deal with crime, not with disinformation. No instrument governs the accountability of platforms, synthetic media or the retreat of multilateralism itself.
regulate.binding_or_powers: Binding on rights; soft on the risk itself
regulate.status: Any rule is in tension with the protection of free expression.

finance.mechanisms: The UN Democracy Fund and the International Programme for the Development of Communication of UNESCO are both small and general.

enforce.mechanisms: The views of the Human Rights Committee are not binding. The Universal Periodic Review is peer review without sanction.

risks.in_practice: This multiplier weakens every other regime, and the gap is almost total. In the UN Global Risk Report 2026, mis- and disinformation is still the most imminent risk, the collapse of the rule of law is the most connected node, and confidence in the capacity of institutions to reduce risk fell for 23 of 28 risks.
risks.gap: Everything is missing except human rights law. The weakness of this multiplier helps to explain the weakness of the others.

risks.name: AI as amplifier

assess.mechanisms: The bodies listed for uncontrolled advanced AI also apply here: the UN Scientific Panel on AI, the International AI Safety Report and the network of AI safety institutes. None of them assesses the link between AI and biological weapons or between AI and nuclear weapons specifically. The summits on Responsible AI in the Military Domain (The Hague 2023, Seoul 2024, A Coruña 2026) discuss military AI.

regulate.mechanisms: The Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (128 parties) has discussed lethal autonomous weapons systems for more than a decade. At its Seventh Review Conference in Geneva (16 to 21 November 2026), the parties did not agree to start negotiations on a binding instrument. They gave a group of governmental experts a new mandate for 2027 and 2028 to develop 'an international instrument', without deciding whether it will be legally binding. More than 95 states supported a binding instrument. Russia blocked consensus, and the United States and several other military powers also opposed binding rules. In October 2026, 163 states backed a resolution in the First Committee of the UN General Assembly that calls for negotiations. Soft law consists of General Assembly resolution 79/239 on AI in the military domain (December 2024), the Blueprint for Action of the Seoul summit (2024, about 60 endorsers, without China) and a political declaration on the responsible military use of AI led by the United States (about 58 endorsers). At the third summit, in A Coruña in February 2026, the United States and China did not endorse the declaration. The Wassenaar Arrangement (42 members) coordinates export controls on dual-use goods, including some computing hardware; controls on advanced chips are national. Nothing covers AI in nuclear command and control. Nothing covers the design of pathogens with AI: the Biological Weapons Convention is silent, and the screening commitments of frontier AI companies are private.
regulate.coverage: Broad (128 parties to the weapons convention); club (others)
regulate.binding_or_powers: Soft law. A mandate to negotiate binding rules was blocked in November 2026.
regulate.status: Talks on autonomous weapons continue until 2028 without a commitment to a treaty.

finance.mechanisms: None.

enforce.mechanisms: None.

risks.in_practice: This is the fastest-rising multiplier, and it is governed by declarations. In 2026 the attempt to start treaty negotiations on autonomous weapons failed, and the two leading AI powers stayed outside the main declaration on military AI.
risks.gap: The links between AI and nuclear weapons and between AI and biological weapons fall between the nuclear, biological and AI regimes. No regime owns them. There are still no binding rules on autonomous weapons.
risks.maturity_note: The trend moved from strengthening to stable in November 2026, when the mandate to negotiate a treaty on autonomous weapons was blocked.
